A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Community Alignment study. Their main text, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and relocated material can be reliably matched.

before.justification: V2 reports an original 15,000-participant survey, evaluations of 21 LLMs, preference-learning experiments and dataset analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and reports a second dataset-collection wave with updated demographic outcomes.

M1.justification: The negatively-correlated sampling prompts, GPT-4o judging procedures and prompt-steering, SFT, DPO and GRPO procedures remain unchanged. The additional recruitment does not introduce a new model or algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same five countries, five languages, chatbot use cases, value dimensions and PRISM-based preference-learning tasks. The second collection wave changes sample composition within existing populations rather than introducing new coverage.

E2.justification: The same prompt-steering, SFT, SFT+DPO and SFT+GRPO comparisons use single-model temperature sampling, temperature sampling from 21 models and single-model NC sampling. The two Llama models and original-model comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The reported dataset collection expands from one wave to two, with the second targeting underrepresented groups. Annotators increase from 3,196 to 3,603, and balanced subsets extend from three countries to all five, allowing a 10% margin for older participants in France and Italy. This substantially revises collection and subset construction; the existing model-training and evaluation protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The temperature-sensitivity study, default-response inclusion check, judge-validation confusion matrices and qualitative case studies are retained. V3's new Appendix D reproduces the existing steering results rather than adding an ablation or robustness experiment.

E5.justification: V3 Figure 3 explicitly identifies steering error bars as standard errors of the mean; v2 Table 1 reports the same uncertainty values without defining them. The 20-generation repetition information is unchanged, and no additional runs or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Reported dataset comparisons increase from 192,137 to 233,319, non-English annotations from 63% to 66%, and feedback availability from 28% to 44%, alongside extensive demographic updates. Figure 2 revises secular-rational and traditional coverage values; v3 reports mean traditional/survival coverage of 15%/30% with temperature sampling and 60%/53% with NC sampling. All 96 steering means and uncertainty values remain identical between v2 Table 1 and v3 Table D.1.

T1.justification: The scoring definitions, explanation of negatively-correlated sampling and GRPO outline are retained. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or substantively revised.

C1.justification: The four central contributions remain intact. V3 expands the dataset contribution to balanced subsets in all five countries and explicitly adds many conversations per annotator as a fifth design attribute supporting personalization.

C2.justification: The representativeness discussion changes from an inability to construct balanced France/Italy subsets to qualified success with a 10% older-age margin. V3 also explicitly connects greater per-annotator conversation history to personalization. Limitations concerning education, political orientation, value dimensions and automated judging remain.

D1.justification: V3 documents the second collection wave's dates and targeting, adds a wave field to the codebook, corrects the assigned_lang description and changes annotator_age's documented type from integer to categorical. These are limited reproducibility and documentation updates; model implementation details and dataset access information are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds Jiang et al.'s Artificial Hivemind work and discusses its Infinity-Chat findings in Appendix A as complementary evidence of output homogeneity. The broader positioning relative to pluralistic alignment and preference datasets remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Related work is substantially condensed and moved from Section 2 to Section 5, while its detailed discussion remains in Appendix A. Other changes include localized wording edits, the fifth dataset attribute, appendix renumbering and codebook reordering; most scientific prose is retained.

P2.justification: The principal steering table is replaced in the main text by an eight-panel bar chart, with the complete table retained in Appendix D. The conversation-count histogram is redrawn with median and tail annotations, Figure 2's caption is revised, and the codebook is reorganized. These materially change presentation of the central results and dataset.

improvement.justification: Targeted recruitment addresses v2's inability to construct balanced France/Italy subsets, while Figure 3 and its uncertainty label improve interpretation of retained results. Documentation remains imperfect: under the per-turn counting that reconciles v2, v3 Appendix I implies 253,254 nonmissing preferences rather than the reported 233,319 comparisons. The dataset and presentation gains are positive but tempered by this unresolved reporting discrepancy.
